title: Day 1 Check: Playbook, OOP & SOLID
summary: Scenario questions the way interviewers ask them. 70% to pass.

questions.q: You're 12 minutes into a 45-minute OOD round. You have a polished class diagram but no code. What's the best move?
options: Add sequence diagrams for every use case so the design is complete
Say which parts are good enough, pick the main use case, and start coding the central service top-down
Ask more clarifying questions to be sure the requirements are right
Refactor the diagram to add more design patterns
questions.explain: The most common no-hire reason is not finishing a working core. Move to code for the main flow and come back to detail later.

questions.q: Which clarifying question changes the design the most for a movie-ticket booking system?
options: What colour scheme should the seat map use?
Should I use Java 17 or Java 21?
Can two users try to book the same seat at the same time, and how long can a seat be held during payment?
How many movies are released per year?
questions.explain: Concurrency on shared resources (seat holds and TTLs) changes the core model and the locking strategy. The other questions don't change any class.

questions.q: `class Penguin extends Bird` and `Penguin.fly()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Which principle is violated, and what's the fix?
options: SRP. Split Penguin into two classes
LSP. Narrow the abstraction (e.g. a separate `Flyable` capability) so callers never get a Bird that can't do what Bird promises
DIP. Inject the flying behaviour
ISP. Make `fly()` return a boolean
questions.explain: A subtype that can't honour the base type's contract breaks Liskov substitution. Fix the hierarchy so the capability is only promised where it exists.

questions.q: `fee(Vehicle v)` contains `switch (v.type()) { case CAR: …; case BIKE: … }` and the product team adds a vehicle type every quarter. Which refactor do interviewers want to see?
options: Add a `default` branch that throws
Move the switch into a static utility class
Make the fee polymorphic (a method on each vehicle type or a pricing strategy per type), so a new type is a new class and existing code is untouched
Store fees in a `Map<String, Integer>` inside the switch
questions.explain: This is Open/Closed: closed for modification, open for extension. A lookup map can also be fine for pure data. The key point is that adding a type must not mean editing branching logic.

questions.q: Which of these is a **value object** rather than an entity?
options: Order #A-1001
A Driver with id `d-42`
Money(500, "INR")
A ParkingTicket
questions.explain: Money has no identity. Two `Money(500, INR)` are interchangeable, and it should be immutable. The others keep their identity across state changes.

questions.q: In Go, `type Admin struct { User }`. Which statement is true?
options: Admin is a subtype of User and can be passed to `func f(u User)`
User's methods are promoted onto Admin, but an Admin is not a User. Polymorphism needs an interface both satisfy
Embedding copies User's fields but not its methods
Go forbids embedding structs that have methods
questions.explain: Embedding is composition with method promotion, not inheritance. To substitute, accept an interface that both types implement.

questions.q: `OrderService` has `private final EmailSender sender = new SmtpEmailSender("smtp.prod");`. What's the main problem an interviewer will point out?
options: It should be `static`
High-level policy depends on a concrete low-level detail, so you can't test it or swap it. Inject an interface through the constructor (DIP)
SMTP is outdated
The field should be public for flexibility
questions.explain: Constructor injection of an abstraction is the standard fix. It's also what makes the code unit-testable with a fake sender.

questions.q: What does the filled-diamond arrow `Lot ◆── Floor` say in a class diagram?
options: Floor inherits from Lot
Lot uses Floor temporarily inside one method
Composition: Lot owns its Floors, and they don't exist without it
Floor implements the Lot interface
questions.explain: A filled diamond is composition, ownership with a shared lifecycle. A hollow diamond is aggregation, where the part has an independent lifecycle.

questions.q: Code does `if (acct.getBalance() >= amt) acct.setBalance(acct.getBalance() - amt);` in a service. Best critique?
options: Fine as is. Services own the logic
It breaks encapsulation (ask instead of tell). `Account.withdraw(amt)` should enforce its own invariant, which also lets you make it atomic
Use floating point for money
Replace with a Singleton account manager
questions.explain: Invariants belong with the data. Putting withdraw on Account removes duplication and gives you one place to add locking.

questions.q: Your logic calls `System.currentTimeMillis()` / `time.Now()` deep inside a pricing method. Why do experienced interviewers dislike that?
options: It's slow
It hides a dependency. Time-based behaviour (hourly fees, TTL expiry) becomes untestable. Inject a clock
It returns UTC
It isn't thread-safe
questions.explain: Treat time and randomness as injected dependencies, so tests can control them. Several exercises in this course rely on this.
